claim: 8-oxodeoxyguanosine (8-oxodG) is one of the major oxidised bases in DNA or the nucleotide pool.
source: 8-oxodeoxyguanosine (8-oxodG) is one of the major oxidised bases in DNA or the nucleotide pool (Kamiya, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kamiya, 2003

claim: Base damage is caused by highly reactive free radicals.
source: Base damage is caused by highly reactive free radicals (Kasai and Nishimura, 1984; Burrows and Muller, 1998; Neeley and Essigmann, 2006; Cadet et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: The repair of 8-oxodG in DNA utilises the base excision repair (BER) pathway, which is evolutionarily conserved from Bacteria to eukaryotes.
source: Evolutionarily conserved from Bacteria to eukaryotes, the repair of 8-oxodG in DNA utilises the base excision repair (BER) pathway, ensuring the removal of dC:8-oxodG and dA:8-oxodG mispairs respectively by OGG1/MutM (Fpg) and MUTYH/MutY BER glycosylases in eukaryotic/E. coli cells.
evidence: Draws from established scientific consensus about BER pathway conservation

claim: The nucleotides dAMP and dCMP are incorporated opposite template 8-oxodG to varying efficiencies, potentially causing dG→dT transversion mutations during subsequent rounds of DNA replication.
source: The nucleotides dAMP and dCMP are incorporated opposite template 8-oxodG to varying efficiencies, potentially causing dG→dT transversion mutations during subsequent rounds of DNA replication (Hübscher and Maga, 2011; Berquist and Wilson, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hübscher and Maga, 2011 and Berquist and Wilson, 2012

claim: The premutagenicity of 8-oxodG in DNA is mainly due to its Hoogsteen base pairing in the syn conformation with dA.
source: The premutagenicity of 8-oxodG in DNA is mainly due to its Hoogsteen base pairing in the syn conformation with dA (Chemical structure 1) and the ability of DNA pols to extend the resulting mismatch (Shibutani et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shibutani et al., 1991 and Chemical structure 1 showing the base pairing

claim: Pyrococcus abyssi has been isolated from hydrothermal vents characterised by elevated temperatures, pH-shifts, radiation and differing metal concentrations.
source: The hyperthermophilic anaerobic Euryarchaea, Pyrococcus abyssi, has been isolated from hydrothermal vents characterised by elevated temperatures, pH-shifts, radiation and differing metal concentrations (Erauso et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citation to Erauso et al., 1993

claim: P. abyssi exhibits extreme resistance to ionising radiation.
source: It exhibits extreme resistance to ionising radiation (Jolivet et al., 2003)
evidence: Supported by citation to Jolivet et al., 2003

claim: P. abyssi can withstand a moderate level of genomic abasic sites damage (25 abasic sites per 100000 bp).
source: can withstand a moderate level of genomic abasic sites damage (25 abasic sites per 100000 bp) (Palud et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Palud et al., 2008

claim: P. abyssi encodes two replicative DNA polymerases, a B-family and a D-family.
source: P. abyssi encodes two replicative DNA polymerases, a B-family and a D-family, which have both been functionally and structurally characterized alone or in the presence of replication factors (Henneke et al., 2005; Rouillon et al., 2007; Castrec et al., 2009; Gouge et al., 2012; Henneke, 2012; Masuda et al., 2015; Sauguet et al., 2016; Lemor et al., 2018; Raia et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations documenting characterization of these polymerases

claim: Both PolD and PolB contain exonuclease domains and display high nucleotide selectivity.
source: Both PolD and PolB contain exonuclease domains and display high nucleotide selectivity (Palud et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citation to Palud et al., 2008

claim: PolB is described as one of the most accurate and processive enzymes.
source: with PolB described as one of the most accurate and processive enzymes (Dietrich et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dietrich et al., 2002

claim: The DNA polymerase/primase complex (p41/p46) is devoid of any proofreading 3'−5' exonuclease activity.
source: Devoid of any proofreading 3'−5' exonuclease activity, it has been identified as an RNA priming enzyme at the replication fork, and a potential DNA repair enzyme capable of synthesising short-patches of DNA (Le Breton et al., 2007; Jozwiakowski et al., 2015; Lemor et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Le Breton et al., 2007; Jozwiakowski et al., 2015; Lemor et al., 2018

claim: In the exponential phase, 63.2 8-oxodG/10^6 dG was calculated for the P. abyssi genome.
source: In the exponential phase, 63.2 8-oxodG/106 dG was calculated for the P. abyssi genome, with the value moderately increasing to 115.1 8-oxodG/106 dG at the stationary phase.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements presented in Table 1

claim: The steady-state level of 8-oxodG in P. abyssi genome moderately increases to 115.1 8-oxodG/10^6 dG at the stationary phase.
source: In the exponential phase, 63.2 8-oxodG/106 dG was calculated for the P. abyssi genome, with the value moderately increasing to 115.1 8-oxodG/106 dG at the stationary phase.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements presented in Table 1

claim: 8-oxodG was not detectable in the genome of E. coli in both exponential and stationary phases of growth.
source: Comparatively, 8-oxodG was not detectable in the genome of E. coli in both phases of growth.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements presented in Table 1

claim: Oxygen sparging of exponentially growing P. abyssi culture for 5 min gave rise to increased levels of genomic 8-oxodG.
source: Oxygen sparging of exponentially growing culture for 5 min gave rise to increased levels of genomic 8-oxodG (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1

claim: The level of 8-oxodG after oxygen exposure (174.9 8-oxodG/10^6 dG at time T1) was approximately 3-fold higher than observed before air exposure (60.1 8-oxodG/10^6 dG at time T0).
source: The level (174.9 8-oxodG/106 dG at time T1) was approximately 3-fold higher than observed before air exposure (60.1 8-oxodG/106 dG at time T0).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1

claim: After 5 min of oxygen exposure, approximately 12% of P. abyssi cells were viable.
source: After 5 min (time T1), approximately 12% of the cells were viable as observed by a lower cell density (7.5 × 106 cells/mL compared with 9.3 × 107 cells/mL at time T0).
evidence: Supported by cell viability measurements shown in Figure 1

claim: After 140 min following oxygen exposure (time T3), P. abyssi achieved complete recovery of the basal level of 8-oxodG (65.1 8-oxodG/10^6 dG).
source: After 140 min (time T3), the number of cells increased to 9.3 × 104 cells/mL. Concomitantly with active cell proliferation, a complete recovery of the basal level of 8-oxodG was obtained (65.1 8-oxodG/106 dG at time T3).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1

claim: P. abyssi possesses the necessary molecular mechanisms to overcome the presence of genomic 8-oxodG.
source: Taken together, these data provide the evidence for the first time that the hyperthermophile anaerobe P. abyssi possesses the necessary molecular mechanisms to overcome the presence of genomic 8-oxodG.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data showing recovery of basal 8-oxodG levels after oxidative stress

claim: P. abyssi can withstand oxidative stress by counteracting and rapidly returning to the basal level of 8-oxodG in DNA.
source: Moreover, P. abyssi can withstand oxidative stress by counteracting and rapidly returning to the basal level of 8-oxodG in DNA.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing recovery of basal 8-oxodG levels within 140 minutes

claim: PabCE is capable of extending primers when presented with dG control in the template strand, with products ranging from 18 to 87nt in length.
source: Using a DNA substrate with a primer-template conformation (p/t-1), it was observed that PabCE is capable of extending primers when presented with dG control in the template strand, with products ranging from 18 to 87nt in length (3% of primers being extended to full length (87nt)).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: When PabCE encounters both an abasic site (AP) and 8-oxodG in template strand DNA, a total arresting of DNA polymerisation one base upstream of the damage base (32nt) is observed.
source: However, when encountering both an abasic site (AP) and 8-oxodG in template strand DNA, a total arresting of DNA polymerisation one base upstream of the damage base (32nt) is observed.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Lack of primer extension by PabCE at damaged sites was due to highly specific nuclease activity, resulting in cleavage of the phosphodiester bond of the damaged nucleotide before it was encountered by the polymerisation enzyme.
source: Rather than being an indication of TLS failure by the replication machinery, lack of primer extension was due to highly specific nuclease activity, resulting in cleavage of the phosphodiester bond of the damaged nucleotide before it was encountered by the polymerisation enzyme (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Low, yet visible levels of TLS by PabCE were observed when 8-oxodG was incorporated within a region of double stranded DNA (p/t-2), with 1% of primer DNA being fully extended in oxidative damage containing substrates.
source: Altering the DNA substrate to incorporate the 8-oxodG within a region of double stranded DNA (p/t-2) enabled low, yet visible levels of TLS by PabCE, with 1% of primer DNA being fully extended in oxidative damage containing substrates, as opposed to 2% for the dG containing substrate (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Encountering template strand 8-oxodG noticeably stalls primer extension by each of the three replicative enzymes (PolB, PolD, p41/p46) compared to the dG control.
source: For each of the enzymes it was observed that encountering template strand 8-oxodG noticeably stalls primer extension compared to the dG control (Figure 3A)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Each of the three replicative enzymes (PolB, PolD, p41/p46) possesses a unique stall profile when encountering 8-oxodG.
source: with each enzyme possessing a unique stall profile that is particularly apparent at the 10 min time point (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: PolB arrests replication one nucleotide upstream of the 8-oxodG (32nt – 9%) or after having based paired a nucleotide opposite 8-oxodG (33nt – 9%).
source: PolB arrests replication one nucleotide upstream of the 8-oxodG (32nt – 9%) or after having based paired a nucleotide opposite 8-oxodG (33nt – 9%).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B-C

claim: PolD stalls following base pairing opposite the 8-oxodG lesion (33nt – 14%) while also exhibiting downstream stalling after encountering 8-oxodG (7% at both 35 or 36nt position).
source: PolD stalls following base pairing opposite the lesion (33nt – 14%, Figure 3B–C) while also exhibiting downstream stalling after encountering 8-oxodG (7% at both 35 or 36nt position)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B-C

claim: 8-oxodG itself has no observable impact on upstream primer extension or during incorporation opposite it by p41/p46.
source: Despite the total impact of 8-oxodG induced blockage for p41/p46 at 10 min being of a similar level to that observed for PolD (Figure 3C), 8-oxodG itself has no observable impact on upstream primer extension or during incorporation opposite it.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: p41/p46 exhibits more pronounced stalling at one (34nt) or two (35nt) nucleotides downstream of the damaged nucleotide.
source: The enzyme partially arrests one nucleotide upstream of the 8-oxodG (32nt), but this is comparable to that observed for the dG control template, with more pronounced stalling seen at one (34nt) or two (35nt) nucleotides downstream of the damaged nucleotide (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B-C

claim: In the presence of RPA, primer extension by both PolB and PolD is initially inhibited, leading to an almost universal loss of full-length primer extension and shorter extension products over 15 min.
source: Here we report that in the presence of RPA primer extension by both PolB and PolD is initially inhibited, leading to an almost universal loss of full-length primer extension and shorter extension products over 15 min, with the same effect observed in the presence of 8-oxodG (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Under standing start conditions with 8-oxodG at the +1 position, RPA causes primer utilisation to decrease by over 50% for both PolB and PolD.
source: Under standing start conditions, with 8-oxodG placed at the +1 position from the primer-template junction, the influence of RPA is more pronounced causing primer utilisation to decrease by over 50% for both PolB and PolD (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: Although RPA doesn't enhance primer utilisation by p41/p46, it does result in longer elongation products.
source: Although RPA doesn't enhance primer utilisation by p41/p46, it does result in longer elongation products, partially mitigating the inhibition that the regulatory p46 subunit exhibits on extension activity (Le Breton et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and citation to Le Breton et al., 2007

claim: The presence of RPA largely alleviates any negative impact that 8-oxodG plays on stalling p41/p46 extension.
source: The presence of RPA largely alleviates any negative impact that 8-oxodG plays on stalling p41/p46 extension, with the previously observed downstream stalling removed in both running start and standing start extension reactions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: Under running start conditions, PolD exhibits a reduction in primer+n formation in the presence of PCNA independently of 8-oxodG in the template strand.
source: Under running start conditions, PolD exhibits a reduction in primer+n formation in the presence of PCNA independently of 8-oxodG in the template strand (27% primer+n formation with PCNA compared to 68% without, for p/t-1 (dG) extension).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D

claim: PCNA stimulates full-length DNA synthesis rather than primer utilisation by PolD.
source: These results are in agreement with our previous data, showing that dNTP incorporation is less efficient on templates annealed to shorter DNA primers and that PCNA stimulates full-length DNA synthesis rather than primer utilisation by PolD (Henneke et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Henneke et al., 2005 and current experimental observations

claim: PolB and p41/p46 exhibit increased primer elongation when reactions are supplemented with PCNA.
source: PolB and p41/p46 exhibit increased primer elongation when reactions are supplemented with PCNA, corresponding to the accumulation of 87nt (PolB) or ~82 nt (p41/p46) products in length (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D

claim: In the context of 8-oxodG bypass, all three polymerisation enzymes benefit from the addition of PCNA, with the % of stalled extension product being reduced.
source: In the context of 8-oxodG bypass, all three polymerisation enzymes benefit from the addition of PCNA, with the % of stalled extension product being reduced, most likely due to the enhanced stability and processivity that PCNA provides (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and inference about PCNA function

claim: For PolB, the combined presence of both PCNA and RPA exacerbates PolB stalling in the presence of 8-oxodG.
source: For PolB the combined presence of both PCNA and RPA, while reducing the processivity enhancements that PCNA alone brings to PolB function, actually exacerbate PolB stalling in the presence of 8-oxodG (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D

claim: For PolD, the overall impact of both RPA and PCNA together is negative, with polymerisation reduced to unobservable levels at 15 min.
source: For PolD the overall impact of both RPA and PCNA together is negative. This is most apparent in PolD when polymerisation is reduced to unobservable levels at 15 min.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D

claim: PCNA and RPA enhance the primer extension activity of the p41/p46 complex and remove any 8-oxodG induced downstream stalling.
source: Again, in contrast to the results observed with the two replicative DNA Pols, PCNA and RPA enhance the primer extension activity of the p41/p46 complex and remove any 8-oxodG induced downstream stalling (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: All three DNA polymerisation enzymes provide correct incorporation opposite the dG control.
source: In this context, it is observed that all three DNA polymerisation enzymes provide correct incorporation opposite the dG control.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4

claim: When incorporating opposite 8-oxodG, all three enzymes are potentially mutagenic with dAMP and dCMP preferentially inserted.
source: Conversely, when incorporating opposite 8-oxodG all three enzymes are potentially mutagenic with dAMP and dCMP preferentially inserted.

claim: PolB suffers from a marked decrease in incorporation levels opposite 8-oxodG, with 35% and 31% primer+n for dAMP and dCMP respectively, compared to 91% dCMP incorporation opposite dG.
source: PolB suffers from a marked decrease in incorporation levels opposite 8-oxodG, with 35% and 31% primer+n for dAMP and dCMP respectively, compared to 91% dCMP incorporation opposite dG.

source: PolD also shows a decreased incorporation when encountering 8-oxodG, 41% and 45% primer+n for dAMP and dCMP respectively, compared to 60% dCMP incorporation opposite dG.

claim: For the p41/p46 complex, the levels of incorporation are similar regardless of the presence of oxidative damage, with 64% and 72% primer+n for dAMP and dCMP respectively, compared to 79% dCMP incorporation opposite dG.

claim: For PolB, primer+n formation occurs regardless of the presence of 8-oxodG, with the lowest activity observed in the presence of dC:8-oxodG (52% primer+n) compared to dA:8-oxodG (73% primer+n) and the dC:dG control (87% primer+n) at the 0.5 min time point.
source: For PolB primer+n formation occurs regardless of the presence of 8-oxodG, with the lowest activity observed in the presence of dC:8-oxodG (52% primer+n) compared to dA:8-oxodG (73% primer+n) and the dC:dG control (87% primer+n) at the 0.5 min time point.

claim: PolD appears less tolerant of 8-oxodG base pairs, with primer+n formation after 0.5 min of 27% and 12% with dA and dC paired opposite 8-oxodG, compared to the dC:dG control (49% primer+n).
source: PolD appears less tolerant of 8-oxodG base pairs, with primer+n formation after 0.5 min of 27% and 12% with dA and dC paired opposite 8-oxodG, compared to the dC:dG control (49% primer+n).

claim: The p41/p46 complex proves more tolerant of the presence of 8-oxodG paired termini, with high levels of primer+n formation at 0.5 min of 69% (dA:8-oxodG) and 65% (dC:8-oxodG), compared to 83% primer+n for the dC:dG control.
source: The p41/p46 complex proves more tolerant of the presence of 8-oxodG paired termini, with high levels of primer+n formation at 0.5 min of 69% (dA:8-oxodG) and 65% (dC:8-oxodG), compared to 83% primer+n for the dC:dG control.

claim: The p41/p46 complex was unable to extend a dT:dG mismatch.
source: Unlike PolB and polD, the p41/p46 complex was unable to extend a dT:dG mismatch.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: There is a marked difference in the exonuclease activity of PolB and PolD regardless of the base contained in the +1 nt position from the primer-template junction.
